Cybersecurity: CrowdStrike in talks to buy Zscaler, target's shares jump 18% amid tech sell-off

On Friday, November 20, Bloomberg and Reuters reported that CrowdStrike, the US cybersecurity giant valued at $235 billion, is in talks to acquire Zscaler, which is worth about $32 billion. Zscaler shares jumped 17% to 18% after the close, while CrowdStrike lost more than 8% [1][2].
According to Bloomberg and Reuters, CrowdStrike and Zscaler are in acquisition talks. No price has been mentioned, neither company has confirmed, and the negotiations could still fall through [1][2].
After Friday's close, Zscaler shares gained about 17% to 18% [1][2]. CrowdStrike fell more than 8% according to Reuters and CNBC [1][2], and about 5% according to FX Leaders [5].
At Friday's close, Zscaler had a market value of about $32 billion and CrowdStrike about $235 billion, more than seven times as much, according to CNBC [1].
The rationale, according to Reuters: large corporate customers want fewer security vendors, and Zscaler would fill CrowdStrike's gap in network protection [2][3].
The deal would allow CrowdStrike to compete more directly with Palo Alto Networks, the leader that already sells a complete offering [3][4]. The two companies are currently partners [4].
It would be one of the largest deals in the history of cybersecurity [6].
Software deals have come in quick succession this week: on November 19, the fund TPG and Corpay agreed to buy BILL for $6 billion, at a 31% premium [7].

Key takeaway: as tech stocks tumble, the strongest companies are taking advantage of lower prices to buy their rivals. For Zscaler, the news lifts the share price; for CrowdStrike, the market is worried about the price it will have to pay [1][2].

Cybersecurity is in a race to become a "platform": a single vendor that protects computers, the "cloud" and networks at the same time. CrowdStrike is strong in protecting computers and servers, Zscaler in secure access to networks and the internet. Together, they would offer the complete range customers are asking for [2][3].

The market reaction is classic: the target's shares rise towards the expected price, while the buyer's fall, because its shareholders fear it will overpay, either in cash or in new shares that dilute their stake [1][2][5].

With a value of $32 billion before any premium, an acquisition would probably cost much more, which would place the deal among the largest in the sector [1][6]. Until anything is signed, the gap between Zscaler's share price and a possible purchase price measures the market's doubts.

You may not know these names, but they protect the computers of many large companies, banks and government agencies. If you have a fund tracking the Nasdaq or US tech, it often holds both stocks: the same news can make one gain and the other lose.

Lufthansa loses €20 million a month and cuts 1,000 jobs in Frankfurt and Munich, pilots threaten to strike from Monday

In a letter to employees, Lufthansa Airlines' management announced the elimination of 1,000 full-time positions at its two main airports, Frankfurt and Munich. The airline lost an average of €20 million a month from January to September. Pilots have given it an ultimatum expiring on November 23 [1][3][7].
"At our Frankfurt and Munich hubs, we now plan to cut a total of 1,000 full-time positions at Lufthansa Airlines," the letter says, about 2.5% of its roughly 40,000 employees [1].
The letter is signed by Jens Ritter, head of Lufthansa Airlines, and four other executives. It does not specify the timetable, the departments affected or how the jobs will be cut [4].

Over the first nine months of 2026, the airline posted an operating loss (adjusted EBIT) of €180 million, or €20 million a month. Management considers it "not competitive" in terms of costs, efficiency and productivity [5].

Lufthansa also wants to shrink its Airbus A320 fleet, partly replaced by more fuel-efficient A220s, and is considering further cuts to short- and medium-haul flights [1][3]. Fuel prices are a heavy burden [6].

In Frankfurt, the organization of connecting flight "waves" will be overhauled, and the technical and administrative departments of the three airlines based in Munich and Frankfurt will be merged, with more automation and artificial intelligence [5].

Swiss, Austrian and Brussels Airlines are not affected [1]. It is unclear whether these jobs come on top of the 4,000 cuts, mostly administrative, announced by the group in September 2025 for 2030 [1][4].

The pilots' union Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) no longer considers itself bound by the no-strike obligation after seven months of fruitless mediation [8]. It is demanding a document of principles by Monday, November 23; otherwise, new strikes are possible [7][9].
Key takeaway: Germany's largest airline is losing money on its core business and cutting staff, just as it risks a new conflict with its pilots [5][7].

On Tuesday, Lufthansa presented an offer based on the mediators' recommendations, with up to 1,000 pilot hires by the end of 2033. The VC rejects it: Arne Karstens, chair of its collective bargaining committee, accuses management of acting as if "seven months of talks had never taken place" [8].
The pilots' last walkout was in April, for the company's centenary [8]. The VC has not announced a strike at this stage, but the ultimatum comes in the middle of the winter booking season [9].

Management itself acknowledges a fundamental problem: costs that are too high and productivity that is too low, made worse by fuel prices [5][6]. The plan to cut 4,000 jobs by 2030 has therefore not been enough to turn around the group's main airline [1].

If you have a Lufthansa flight or a connection in Frankfurt or Munich in the coming weeks, keep an eye on the news from Monday: a pilots' strike could cancel flights. In the event of a cancellation, the airline must offer you a refund or re-routing.

Hormuz: Qatari mediators in Tehran, but Iran readies more than 14 tankers to break the US blockade

A Qatari delegation spent two hours in Tehran on the evening of Friday, November 20, trying to revive diplomacy between Iran and the United States. At the same time, Iran is calling the US naval blockade an "act of war" and is gathering more than 14 tankers at Kharg, its main oil terminal, in an attempt to break it [1][3][6].

"A Qatari delegation came to Tehran last night and we held two hours of consultations," Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran's deputy foreign minister, said on Saturday. The content of the talks was not disclosed [1][2].

According to him, Tehran is talking with mediators, including the Qataris, "both in person and remotely", but these contacts are not yet formal negotiations. Iran will reopen Hormuz once Washington has met its "demands", he said [1][5].

Kazem Gharibabadi also called the US blockade an "act of war" and promised that Iran would take "any necessary measure" to break it [3][4]. He set three conditions: lifting the blockade, unfreezing Iranian assets held abroad and ending the war on all fronts [4].

According to satellite images and ship-tracking data cited by Euronews, Iran has placed crews aboard more than 14 tankers at Kharg and raised its flag on them; a convoy could set off towards the Gulf of Oman in the coming days. Tehran has made no official announcement [6].

Media outlets linked to the Revolutionary Guards, including the Fars agency, are threatening to strike oil facilities in the Gulf, "especially the oil of the Emirates", if the convoy is attacked [6][7]. Two more tankers were hit in the strait, according to the British maritime agency UKMTO, and Bahrain says it intercepted Iranian attacks [8].
On the US side, Donald Trump told Fox News that Iran wants a deal, but is demanding a durable agreement that would bind even his successors, warning that the war will end "one way or another" [3][9].

Key takeaway: diplomacy and escalation are moving forward at the same time. Qatar is keeping a channel open, but if Iran sends its tankers against the blockade, the US Navy will have to choose between letting them through and stopping them, at the risk of retaliation against oil terminals in the Gulf [1][6][7].

The stakes are vital for Tehran: before the war, about 90% of the crude oil exported by Iran passed through Kharg, and that flow has almost stopped since the United States reimposed the blockade on July 14 [6][7]. The war itself was triggered in February by US and Israeli attacks on Iran [1].
Qatar has been acting as an intermediary for months: its prime minister came to Tehran on August 27, and a Qatari delegation was already there on October 30, with no agreement [10][11].
For now, markets are betting on de-escalation: oil posted its third consecutive weekly decline this week, even as Iran was preparing this convoy [12].

The price you pay to fill up depends partly on what happens in Hormuz. If the Iranian convoy sets off and things get out of hand, oil could rise quickly. If the Qatari mediators secure real negotiations, the decline of recent weeks could continue.

United States: facing an incoming Democratic Congress, Trump offers to work together on healthcare and immigration, but threatens to "block everything" by veto for two years

On Friday, November 20, at the White House, and then on Saturday on Fox News, Donald Trump said he saw a "very good chance" of deals with the Democrats, who will take control of both chambers of Congress in January. But he pointed out that he could "block everything" by veto until the end of his term [1][2][4].

Friday's freewheeling press conference followed a four-day trip to China and the Philippines [5]. Trump said he wanted to use the veto to put pressure on the incoming Democratic majority, while saying he was ready to work with Hakeem Jeffries, the future Speaker of the House [1].

On healthcare: "They want to talk to me about two things in particular: healthcare, because we can do something together," he said, arguing that a compromise would do better than what Republicans had attempted on their own [6].
According to CBS News, he also warned that he would tell the Democrats he will veto their bills if they do not accept his conditions [4].

On Saturday on Fox News, he insisted: "I could sit for two years and a month and veto everything," before adding that nothing would then get done for anyone. He called Hakeem Jeffries a "reasonable guy" [2].

But Hakeem Jeffries had called Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff and architect of its anti-immigration policy, a "stone-cold racist" and said he could not imagine negotiating with him [3]. On Friday, Trump brought Stephen Miller to the podium, called him "the most powerful man in the world" and suggested he run for president in 2028 [1].

In the November 3 midterm elections, the Democrats won both chambers: a provisional count gave them 228 seats in the House and 54 in the Senate, with seven Senate seats taken from Republicans, including Texas, Ohio and North Carolina [7].

Key takeaway: for his last two years, Trump will no longer be able to pass his laws through an allied Congress; he will have to negotiate or block, and he is deliberately keeping both options open [1][2].

The presidential veto allows the president to reject a law passed by Congress; overriding it requires a two-thirds majority in each chamber, far more than the 228 seats out of 435 and 54 seats out of 100 projected for the Democrats [7]. It is therefore the main weapon left to Trump, which he himself presents as a negotiating lever rather than a systematic refusal [2].

Immigration is at the heart of the standoff: ICE deported about 483,200 people in fiscal year 2026, a record (+9%), far from the target of one million; 58% of voters surveyed in exit polls felt the administration had gone too far [8].
The first test will come on January 3, when the new Congress convenes and Hakeem Jeffries must be elected Speaker of the House by a vote of all representatives [7].

What happens in Washington also affects Europe: the budget, tariffs and aid to Ukraine all go through Congress. A president and a Congress that block each other often means fewer decisions and more uncertainty for businesses and markets.

EU budget 2028-2034: Costa proposes nearly €200 billion in cuts and a tax on digital giants, Paris calls the text "very disappointing"

On Saturday, November 21, European Council President António Costa presented a new version of the EU budget for 2028-2034, cut by nearly €200 billion (10%) and partly financed by a 3% tax on digital services. The Élysée immediately rejected it, saying farmers were poorly protected [1][2][3].
The Commission's proposal, presented in 2025, totaled about €2,000 billion over seven years [6]. António Costa's text cuts it by nearly €200 billion, or about 10% [1].

These cuts aim to win over the so-called "frugal" countries, which want to spend less [1]. Germany and Sweden, however, are calling for even more savings, according to the Spanish website Demócrata [5].

To fill the coffers, António Costa proposes a 3% tax on digital services, instead of a tax on large companies deemed too contentious [1]. The text also provides for studying a tax on crypto-assets [6].
The EU's external action (the "Global Europe" program, which notably funds development aid) faces new cuts [4].
The French presidency described the proposal as "deeply disappointing" and said it "does not constitute a basis" for an agreement, because it does not sufficiently protect farmers' incomes [2][3].

António Costa says he is "confident" that his text is "a good basis to move forward" [4]. It will be discussed by heads of state and government at an extraordinary summit on November 26 and 27, with the difficult goal of reaching an agreement by the end of the year [4].
Emmanuel Macron had already warned that an agreement would be politically harder to reach after 2026 [7].
Key takeaway: Europe is negotiating its budget for seven years and the 27 member states are pulling in opposite directions, France to protect agriculture, Germany and Sweden to spend less [2][5].

The multiannual budget sets what the EU will be able to fund from 2028 to 2034: support for farmers (the Common Agricultural Policy), funds for poorer regions, research, defense and external aid. Every euro removed from one line creates winners and losers [1][4].
The 3% digital tax would target the sector's large groups, the so-called "Big Tech" [1][6]. It would replace a tax on large companies that divided capitals too much [1].
Unanimity is required: a single country saying no is enough to block everything. The French refusal, five days before the summit, signals a very tough negotiation [2][4].

This budget partly determines the subsidies French farmers receive, the roads or schools funded in your region and Erasmus grants. If the EU spends less, France will have to choose between making up the difference from its own already very tight budget, or cutting.

After taking Bau, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and their SPLM-N rebel allies say they have captured five localities in southeastern Blue Nile, about forty kilometers from Ed Damazin. Key takeaway: the war between the army and the RSF is spreading to southeastern Sudan, in a region bordering Ethiopia. If Ed Damazin fell, the paramilitaries would gain a foothold in another regional capital [3][5][8].

The sources contradict each other: the RSF claim rapid gains, while the army and the local government speak of propaganda. No independent source confirms the front line, hence the caution about the stated distances [2][5][6].

Blue Nile is also a regional issue: Sudan Tribune reported a military buildup at an Ethiopian base presented as a threat to Ed Damazin, raising fears of a war spilling across borders [10]. Sudan may seem far away, but it is one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, and every new town captured forces thousands of families onto the roads. When two sides give opposing accounts, remember this above all: civilians are fleeing, and that is the most reliable sign that the threat is real.

Taipei has made the review of this special budget a priority [4].
Key takeaway: this vote gives fresh money to Taiwan's military, but the major eight-year arms plan remains blocked by the standoff between President Lai and the opposition [1][2].

Washington has been pressing the island for months to increase its military spending [2][3]: every budget vote is therefore also a message sent to the United States, Taiwan's main military backer, and to Beijing.

news.2026-11-22-colombie-apres-greve-loi: Colombia: after the national strike, the left threatens a "general strike" against Abelardo de la Espriella's fiscal law

The day after the 24-hour strike on November 19 against President Abelardo de la Espriella's "economic rescue law", left-wing Senator Iván Cepeda warned that the country is heading for a general strike if the government refuses dialogue [1][3].
The 24-hour strike was called by the Central Union of Workers (CUT), joined by other unions, students and social organizations, against the bill sent to Congress [1][2].

According to Iván Cepeda, a senator from the Historic Pact, thousands of people marched in Bogotá and other cities; roads were blocked and more than 70,000 public transport users were affected in the capital [3].
He vows to bring down the law "in the streets or in Congress" [3].
The government has dropped some measures, but the unions denounce those that remain in the text: privatizations, cuts to public employment and higher health contributions [4].
Key takeaway: the budget showdown is now moving to Congress, where the bill must be voted on, and the street is threatening to step up the pressure [3][4].

The government has already backed down on part of the text, a sign that the pressure is working [4]. But the unions and the left-wing opposition are demanding the withdrawal of the entire package, and the vote in Congress will show who holds the upper hand [3][4].
Long strikes can disrupt economic activity, but the main issue remains social: who will pay for fixing Colombia's public finances.
